title: Amplifying Talk Impact through Visual Reinforcement
text:
Pixels with Purpose
How to Amplify the Impact of Your Talk Through Visual Reinforcement


Not sure if I love this title, but trying to come up with something that frames the overarching point—that “the slides” are secondary to “the point” and “the narrative”… but they do still matter.
I also spent some time trying to get the “corner” images from the PowerPoint example… and that’s uniquely difficult to pull off in Quarto.

title: Amplifying Talk Impact through Visual Reinforcement
text: The goal of any talk is audience impact.

title: Amplifying Talk Impact through Visual Reinforcement
text:
Slides don’t drive impact.


The talk drives impact.


Slides simply reinforce the talk.



Slides are not where a talk starts.
Verbally: Don’t worry! We WILL talk about slides. We just want to be clear that slides are not where a talk starts.

title: Amplifying Talk Impact through Visual Reinforcement
text:
Hold their attention.


Help them understand what’s being presented.


Enable them to retain what matters most.



Image source: https://unsplash.com/photos/man-standing-beside-rock-formation-mj51pZwan9c?utm_source=unsplash&utm_medium=referral&utm_content=creditShareLink
Ask: What can the slides do better than my words?
“Keep attention” and “Remember it” (Talk can be about caring, attention, multi-encoding)

Keep the audience’s attention — the talk is bound by time and attention
Understand and care about the information — by directly reinforcing what the speaker is saying
Remember it — dual-encoding with multiple senses (hearing and seeing); brain science backs up that using multiple senses aids retention

What slides should not (primarily) do

Remind the speaker what they’re supposed to be saying

Caveat: break in case of emergency… they can be a visual aid to keep the speaker on track; that’s just a natural artifact if they do their primary job well!

title: Amplifying Talk Impact through Visual Reinforcement
text:
Maximize the data-pixel ratio!

This concept was initially put forth by Edward Tufte as “the data-ink ratio,” and Stephen Few later modernized it as “the data-pixel ratio.”




Data-Information Pixels


All Non-Background Pixels



  Every pixel that is notsimply the background color
 Pixels that representactual data or information

Visually define — multiple slides, but they go quick.
Close with, verbally: this is reducing cognitive load by giving the brain fewer decisions to make about “what matters.”

title: Amplifying Talk Impact through Visual Reinforcement
text:
(Increase the data-pixel ratio of) Code!

penguins_clean <- penguins |>
  drop_na(body_mass_g, flipper_length_mm, bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm) |>
  mutate(body_mass_kg = body_mass_g / 1000,
         species = as.factor(species),
         island = as.factor(island),
         sex = as.factor(sex))

model_spec <- lm(body_mass_kg ~ flipper_length_mm + bill_length_mm +
                   bill_depth_mm + species + sex,
                 data = penguins_clean)

model_summary <- broom::tidy(model_spec, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.95)

model_summary |>
  filter(term != "(Intercept)") |>
  arrange(desc(abs(estimate)))


Quick hit: before / after — limit the initial version to JUST be reducing the volume of code shown and making ONE LINE of the code a larger font and bold/black; other code is “context” — smaller font BUT NOT SMALL and lighter color BUT NOT TOO LIGHT such that there is projector risk.
[Placeholder styling note: the “after” treatment below uses Quarto’s code-line-numbers highlighting; a fuller size/color treatment may need SCSS tuning against the syntax highlighter.]

title: Amplifying Talk Impact through Visual Reinforcement
text:
“Brain breaks” can be useful
Brain breaks (Make it interesting to pay attention):

Reveal — show something that is hard to describe (often a moment of revelation)
Explain — images can create connections that words cannot
Delight — aesthetics keep people interested


Gifs, comics, memes, blank screen

For the audience (TED book).
